message.content:
The **earliest surviving reference to Jesus Christ in a non‑Christian historical record** comes from the Jewish historian **Flavius Josephus** in his work *Antiquities of the Jews* (Book 18, Chapter 3). Josephus wrote this text around **93–94 CE**, roughly a decade after Jesus’ death. In the passage—often called the “Testimonium Flavianum”—Josephus describes Jesus as a wise man, a doer of “wonderful works,” and notes that he was crucified under Pontius Pilate at the instigation of the Jewish leaders.

> *“Now there was a wise man named Jesus, who was a doer of wonderful works. He was a teacher of people who were looking for truth. He attracted a large number of followers. He was crucified by Pilate, but the Christians who had followed him did not give up their faith.”* (Josephus, *Antiquities* 18.3.3)

This passage is widely regarded as the earliest independent attestation of Jesus outside the New Testament. It is followed by other Roman sources such as:

| Source | Date | Reference |
|--------|------|-----------|
| **Tacitus** – *Annals* 15.44 | ~116 CE | Mentions “Christus” (Christ) and his execution under Pilate. |
| **Pliny the Younger** – *Letters* 10.96 | ~112 CE | Describes early Christians worshipping Christ. |

While the earliest Christian writings (the Gospel of Mark) are dated to the 60s–70s CE, the first **historical** mention of Jesus outside Christian texts is Josephus’s *Antiquities* from the 90s CE.
